title: AI Interpretation Scope Policy: Stop Criteria and Exceptions
summary: Create an AI interpretation scope policy with approved uses, standing exclusions, temporary stop triggers, patient preference, and handoffs.
body_markdown:
###


No federal rule creates a universal list of encounter types that must use a human interpreter. United States covered entities should evaluate applicable language-access obligations, patient communication needs, organizational policy, and the capabilities tested for the intended workflow without presenting an internal restriction as a legal mandate.


###


A standing exclusion keeps an unapproved language, communication need, device setup, or workflow outside the organization’s current AI scope. A temporary stop trigger pauses an otherwise approved United States healthcare encounter because conditions such as incomplete audio, unresolved speaker identity, or changed clinical meaning prevent reliable communication.


###


No. In a United States language-access program, patient preference is a routing decision, not evidence that the AI system failed. Document the requested method, connect the approved complementary human interpreter pathway, and report preference separately from technical or quality incidents.


###


Not on the update announcement alone. A healthcare organization should retest the affected language, clinical task, delivery channel, and failure conditions, document the results, and obtain approval from the policy owner before expanding its local AI interpretation scope.


###


Staff should document the language, clinical task, observable trigger, attempted correction, alternative method, material information rechecked, and unresolved concern in the organization’s designated record. In a United States covered workflow, avoid copying unnecessary sensitive conversation details into an incident or audit log.
